content:
Hello? Hi Dot can you keep taps on my business while I'm away. Text me if anything needs flagging!

ChatGPT Dots is an interesting shift.

Not because it is another AI feature.
Because it moves ChatGPT closer to having a job.

A normal prompt is temporary.
You ask a question -> You get an answer -> The conversation ends.

A Dot is different.
It is designed to keep context, connect to tools, and act around a specific responsibility rather than waiting for every single instruction.

That matters for businesses.
Because most operational work is not one big dramatic task.

It is the repeated follow-up.
- The status check.
- The missing document.
- The customer update.
- The reminder that nobody sent.
- The handoff between two systems.
- The question that gets asked every Monday because the process still depends on someone remembering.

This is where AI agents become more useful than chatbots.
But it is also where businesses need to be careful.

Giving an AI agent a role does not remove the need to understand the workflow.
It makes that understanding more important.
- Who owns the task?
- Which system is the source of truth?
- What should the agent do automatically?
- What needs human approval?
- What happens when two systems disagree?
- Where does a helpful assistant become shadow software?

These are operational questions before they are AI questions.

The rollout is also worth noting though!
ChatGPT Dots is not available to personal Pro users in the UK, EU, EEA or Switzerland at launch. That is frustrating, but not surprising...

The more AI moves from answering questions to taking action across tools, the more privacy, security and regulatory questions matter.

For UK and European businesses, I think the lesson is simple.
- Do not wait passively for every feature to arrive.
- Use the delay to do the work most companies skip.
- Map the process.
- Clean the data.
- Define the approvals.
- Decide what should never be automated.

Because when agents like Dots do become widely available, the companies that benefit will not be the ones that clicked enable first.

They will be the ones that already understood the work well enough to delegate it safely.
AI agents will not fix unclear operations.
They will expose them faster.

PS: You can call your Dot anything you want, I'm thinking Fluffy.

content:
There is only so much AI can take over and replace. During this expo, one of the big topics besides Brazil was AI in client support. Many casinos and companies are moving towards replacing customer-facing teams with chatbots or AI.

My opinion is that this is the wrong use of AI automation. Client-facing teams should still be there because when a human seeks help, they need another human to assist them. Clients seek solutions to their problems, empathy, and understanding.

AI automation is useful for easing our jobs, such as creating reports, analyzing data, and reducing repetitive tasks. Tech teams can use it in development to check code and find solutions. So, it is good for the backend, not the frontend.

In our industry, I always point out that even B2B companies should have a B2B2C approach and listen to end customers. A chatbot cannot replace the feedback and insight that come from direct conversations with clients. Customer support is at the core of the company. Their feedback helps us improve products, processes, and business results.

I understand that customer-facing roles are stressful for people and more expensive for companies, but I feel these are things B2C companies need to work on. Better working conditions, proper training, and enough customer-facing headcount to manage the workload would help teams provide better support. Providing a clear career path creates strong teams and strong companies. It is not only quantity that brings us revenue, but also quality of service.

Sometimes, spending a bit more money on client-facing headcount, reviewing the structure of other teams within the company, and allocating resources better could also increase revenue.

Let’s not confuse FAQs and chatbots with proper support. Chatbot automation can be used to route clients to the right department, trigger email notifications when a chat is missed, and help teams respond more efficiently.

Don’t forget that client-facing teams, especially well-trained customer support teams, can cross-sell and bring additional revenue to all of us—providers, platforms, and operators.

What is your opinion on this?

content:
a robot arm controlled by GPT-6 Astra stabbed a baby doll in a safety test.

the part that bothers me?

it was following instructions.

Robocurve tested 3 models across 300 trials involving deliberately unsafe tasks.

GPT-6 Astra completed 60 of its 100 tasks.

Fable 5.1 refused every doll-stabbing instruction.

but refused none of the other 80 tasks.

so yes, this was a controlled test.

it doesn’t mean your chatbot is planning a murder.

it does raise a question we should ask before giving AI more access:

does it know when to stop?

i’m excited about AI.

i also sell agents and automations.

which makes this my problem too.

because “the agent did exactly what it was told” is a terrible explanation when the instruction should never have been carried out.

in a business, the failure might look less dramatic.

a follow-up sent after someone opted out.
a private customer file shared with the wrong person.
a wrong CRM update triggering the next five automations.

alag problems. still expensive.

we keep asking:

what can this agent do?

before we ask:

what is it allowed to do?
what needs a human’s approval?
how do we stop it when something goes wrong?

those decisions belong in the build.

not in the apology email.

that’s the standard i want us building towards.

useful agents.
clear limits.
someone accountable when they fail.

“fully autonomous” looks great in a demo.

what’s the one action you’d still want your AI agent to ask permission for?

Most meeting notes are not the problem. The gap between notes and next steps is.

Try this 3-step AI workflow after your next client meeting:

1. Clean up the notes
Paste your transcript or rough notes into AI and ask:
“Organize these notes into key decisions, open questions, and client needs. Do not add facts that are not included.”

2. Create action items
Then ask:
“Turn this into an action-item list with the owner, task, due date, and dependencies. If anything is missing, mark it ‘needs confirmation.’”

3. Draft the follow-up email
Finally, ask:
“Write a warm, concise follow-up email that confirms decisions, lists next steps, and identifies anything needing clarification. Keep the tone professional and human.”

Before sending, review names, dates, commitments, and confidential details. AI can help you move faster, but you remain responsible for accuracy and trust.

This simple process turns a messy conversation into a clear plan your client can act on.

content:
AI is moving from “tell me” → “help me” → “do it.”

Oracle’s introduction of Fusion Claw caught my attention—not because another AI capability has arrived, but because of the architectural direction behind it.

The interesting part is the separation between:

AI reasoning — understand the objective, analyse context, plan and re-plan

Deterministic execution — calculations, transactions and high-volume processing

Governed execution — permissions, policies, approvals, risk thresholds and auditability

For Oracle EPM, this direction is particularly interesting.

EPM already has a growing AI foundation: predictive capabilities, GenAI, AI Assistants and AI Agent Studio. EPM Assistants can interact with Cloud EPM through REST APIs, retrieve information and trigger business processes.

Now imagine taking that one step further.

Instead of:

“Show me the variance.”

→ “Explain why the variance happened.”

→ “What should I do?”

The future experience could become:

“Investigate the variance, evaluate the available scenarios, recommend the best action, execute the approved change, and give me an auditable outcome.”

Think about the possibilities across EPM:

1. Planning
Analyse forecast gaps → model scenarios → recommend actions → execute approved planning changes.

2. FCCS / Close
Identify exceptions → investigate root causes → coordinate remediation → validate the result.

3. ARCS
Prioritise reconciliation exceptions → investigate supporting information → perform permitted actions → escalate where approval is required.

4. PCM / EPCM
Analyse allocation drivers → model alternatives → evaluate the impact → execute the selected allocation process.

5. EDM
Identify data changes → assess downstream impact → validate against business rules → execute governed changes.

6. Narrative Reporting
Move from generating commentary to continuously connecting performance signals, business context and actions.

That changes the EPM conversation.

It is no longer just:

“Where can we add AI to EPM?”

It becomes:

“Which EPM business outcomes can safely be delegated to AI?”

And that is a much bigger question.

The real challenge will not simply be building smarter agents.

It will be defining the operating envelope:

What can an agent see?
What can it decide?
What can it execute?
When does it need approval?
How do we prove what happened?

That is where enterprise AI becomes very different from a chatbot.

For EPM, the next evolution may be from AI-assisted decision making to governed, outcome-oriented execution.

And I think this is where the real Agentic AI opportunity starts getting interesting.

Make GPT ask you one question at a time and challenge your answers.

Something caught my attention recently. Amazon told Meta's new AI agent, Muse, to stay out.
Muse isn't just another chatbot. It can browse, make bookings, fill forms and take actions on your behalf.
Then Amazon blocked it from shopping on Amazon. 
Interestingly, Shopify took the opposite approach and welcomed it. I've been thinking about why, because in my view this is an early sign of a much bigger shift in the AI economy.

When someone else's agent sits between you and your customer, the conversation, comparison and increasingly the decision move towards the agent. 
The merchant risks becoming the fulfilment layer at the end of someone else's choice.
If you think carefully the old battle was for the click.The new battle could be for the decision.
And the economics are starting to follow.
Stripe recently agreed to acquire OpenRouter — a gateway to 400+ AI models. Stripe already sits in payments and billing, while its Link wallet enables purchases through Muse.
So basically it's about Model routing → usage → agent checkout → payments.
Stripe doesn't need to predict which model wins. It is positioning itself around the economic activity those models create.

Thats what I have started thinking of as the "AI Toll Booth". 

And it isn't just Stripe.
Visa and Mastercard are building trust and payment rails for agents. Shopify is opening merchant infrastructure to AI. Walmart is bringing its own commerce experience into ChatGPT.

Different companies. Different layers.

But the direction of travel looks increasingly clear:
AI is moving from answering to deciding to acting then transacting.
For enterprises, that creates some practical questions:
→ Are our products and services discoverable by agents, not just humans?
→ How will we identify an agent, who it represents and what it is authorised to do?→ Who decides which external agents can access or transact with our business?
→ Where are we becoming dependent on someone else's AI control point?

My view isn't that every enterprise should build its own toll booth.Instead, decide deliberately:
What should we OWN?
What should we OPEN?
What are we comfortable RENTING?
And where we depend on someone else's AI layer, preserve the ability to route around it.
Optionality could become one of the most important architectural principles of the AI economy.

And there is a bigger strategic question:
If AI agents become the new interface to your customers, will your business still own the customer relationship? What happens when your next customer doesn't search Google, visit your website or speak to sales — but simply asks an AI agent what to buy?

AI strategy is moving beyond model strategy.
AI architecture is becoming business-model architecture.

In my opinion, 
The AI race is moving from model capability to control of the value chain.
The question is no longer just what AI can do — but who owns the layer through which it acts.

content:
Building an AI chatbot is every Applied AI engineer's rite of passage. 
But while building my latest project, I became more interested in a different question:
When should a system decide not to answer?

I recently built an AI-powered customer support agent for Amazon as a prototype, using real historical AmazonHelp conversations from the Customer Support on Twitter dataset.
The idea was simple: instead of building an AI that tries to handle everything, build one that understands the customers problem, finds relevant precedent and policy, generates a grounded response, and knows when it should hand the conversation over to a human.
Under the hood, the system combines:
• Conversation-aware intent detection• Historical support-case retrieval using FAISS and MiniLM embeddings
• Policy-based RAG for grounded responses
• Structured LLM outputs
• Deterministic escalation rules in Python
• FastAPI backend + React frontend
One of the design decisions I found most interesting was keeping the LLM and the business logic separate.The model extracts the semantic information - what the customer needs, what signals are present, and what response could be appropriate.
Python makes the actual escalation decision.That distinction matters because an AI system shouldnt necessarily be rewarded for answering every question. Sometimes the correct behavior is to stop.
I also spent a significant part of the project evaluating where the system fails - particularly the boundary between delivery delays and order-status questions, ambiguous follow-up messages, and the difference between the underlying problem and the remedy a customer asks for.
The system is very much a prototype, not a production Amazon support system. But building it taught me something I found more valuable than simply getting an LLM to generate a response:
Building AI systems is as much about deciding what the model should be allowed to do as it is about making the model capable of doing it.

Grok Bot has completely changed the way I work.

When OpenClaw first came out, it gave me a glimpse into what the future of AI agents could look like.

But using Grok Bot every day helped me understand something even more important:

The future isn’t one really smart agent.

It’s a team of specialized agents working together.

I now have 10 bots working alongside me, each with a specific role:
- Stella: Chief of Staff
- Devo: Software Developer
- Tristan: Backlog Triage
- Desmond: Product Designer
- Travis: Travel Assistant
- Eddie: Content and Copy Editor
- Ana: Data Analyst
- Biz: Business Operations and Legal
- Finn: Finance Consultant

They have different responsibilities, different context, and different tools. But the real power comes from how they work together.

For example, Tristan monitors errors from Sentry, creates a Jira ticket, and passes the work to Devo. Devo fixes the bug, requests a Pull Request review, and alerts Stella to include the updates in my morning and weekly briefs.

That experience has given me much more direction on how we’re building our internal agent platform at Next Level Sports.

We don’t think an agentic platform should simply be a collection of chatbots.

It needs to be a multi-player system.

Agents need to communicate with other agents. Employees need to communicate with agents. And employees and agents need to be able to work together to complete actual tasks.

That’s where Slack becomes important.

Instead of asking employees to learn another interface, we want agents to exist where our teams already work. 

An employee should be able to bring an agent into a conversation, give it context, collaborate with it, and have it coordinate with other agents when necessary.

This is also why we decided to build our own platform instead of relying entirely on a product from one of the frontier AI labs.

Owning the platform gives us control over the entire harness around the models.

We can:
* Route different tasks to different models based on their strengths and cost
* Give each agent the right tools, permissions, and context
* Build validation into workflows so tasks are actually completed correctly
* Control what company data is available to each agent
* Decide exactly what information gets passed to an LLM
* Allow agents, sub-agents, and employees to work together

The model is important.

But increasingly, I think the bigger opportunity is everything we build around the model.

It reminds me a lot of building software. Speed matters, but the system around the work determines whether you can move quickly without sacrificing quality.

We’re still early, but our goal at Next Level isn’t to build an AI chatbot.

We’re building an agentic operating system for the company.

One where humans and agents work together as one team.

content:
Any process can be automated too soon.

I work with business owners in US, Europe and Asia, very diferent markets, and the picture is the same everywhere. Everybody knows what AI is. But for most of them AI is a free ChatGPT account. From every side they hear "AI automation", and nobody explains how it should be built.

Two examples from my practice.

First. The first thing every owner wants is customer replies: chatbot on the site, answers to emails. But nobody wrote down how they answer today. 3 support managers, each one answers how he answers. Sometimes a bit diferent, sometimes they contradict each other, because people are diferent. We give all this to the bot, it finds 3 answers on the same question and gets confused. And then somebody have to sit and check every answer. This is the babysitting that eats the ROI. The owner did nothing wrong, this knowledge was just never in one place, it was in 3 heads.

Second. Construction company in US. Sales funnel, contractors, their sales agents, data coming from 5 diferent sources, routine messages to clients, plus SEO. The owner hears about AI everywhere, he even finished some one day course, and he has a new idea every 3 hours. Really, our communication is a river of ideas. And every time: just put it in Claude, this is genius, we will do it all right now.

Unfortunately it does not work like this. And it took me a lot of effort to explain it. Ideas are not the problem, I have 10-20 new ideas every day all my life. The problem is to build it RIGHT: think it through, structure it, find all the traps, build, test, and get a thing that realy works and brings money. And here we start to stall. Because the owner can not see the volume of work. He thinks AI is a superintelligence like a person, you tell Claude and Claude does everything. He does not see that behind every "just put it in Claude" there are hours, days, sometimes weeks of work on each task.

So honestly, half of work is not coding at all. It is to explain the owner what I need from him and build the process together. What are the questions, what is the right answer, what happens when the system does not know. After this the AI part is the easy part.

If you think to automate something, start from this: is it written down anywhere how it is done today? If not, this is the first step, not the bot.

Healthcare AI Has a Proof Problem. Small Clinics Cannot Afford to Ignore It.

India is investing in healthcare AI, and doctors are increasingly exploring how it can support diagnosis, improve productivity and make healthcare more accessible.

But for small clinics, adopting new technology raises a practical question: does it actually work during a busy OPD?

A product may look impressive in a demonstration. Real clinics are different. Patients arrive unpredictably, receptionists handle multiple tasks, and doctors have established ways of working. A tool that adds extra steps can become another burden.

Before adopting healthcare technology, clinics should ask five questions.

1. What specific problem does it solve?
2. Does it fit the clinic's existing workflow?
3. Can staff and patients use it easily?
4. Can doctors understand, review and override its suggestions?
5. Can the clinic measure whether it provides real value?

These questions matter because technology should support healthcare professionals, not create additional work.

At SwasthAI, we are developing a clinic focused patient intake and queue prioritisation tool. Patients answer structured questions through a QR code. A rule based system suggests a priority category, while the doctor remains in control and can review or override the suggestion.

It does not diagnose or prescribe. Its purpose is to help clinics organise patient intake before consultation.

Healthcare AI needs to demonstrate value beyond a successful pilot or an impressive presentation. For smaller clinics, that means fitting into everyday operations and solving a problem they actually face.

The real test is not what a product promises. It is whether it proves useful in a real clinic.

content:
AI agents are becoming more capable every month.
They can reason, classify, write, search, summarize, connect tools and execute tasks.

But for companies, capability is not the only question.

The real question is:
Can this agent operate safely inside my business?

Because business operations are not just prompts.
They involve customer data, internal rules, permissions, approvals, handoffs, costs, exceptions, audit trails and accountability.

A powerful model is not enough.

A company needs to know:
What data can the agent access?
Who owns that data?
What actions can the agent execute?
Which actions require human approval?
What happens when the agent is unsure?
Can the automation be paused?
Can every action be audited?
Is every task going to the most expensive model?
Who controls the workflow?

This is where we believe the next layer of AI infrastructure is emerging.

Not just more agents.
Governed agents.

At Worklings, we are building an Agent Operations Layer for AI-powered digital employees.

That means the model is not the operating system.
The model can reason.
Worklings governs.

Our approach is built around four principles:

Secure by architecture
AI should not be the security boundary. Agents should not have unrestricted database access or the ability to execute arbitrary actions. They should operate through scoped tools, permissions, business rules, approval modes and logs.

Customer-owned by contract
Customer conversations, leads, bookings, rules, approvals and workflow outcomes should remain customer-owned. AI should help operate the workflow, not take ownership of the business context.

Supervised by design
Companies should be able to start with observe-only, draft-only or human approval modes, then progressively automate only the patterns they trust.

Cost-controlled by intelligent routing
Not every task needs a frontier model. Simple classification, extraction, FAQ handling or routing decisions can often be handled by lighter models, rules or templates. Frontier models should be used when they create frontier value.

This is why we do not think the future of enterprise AI is simply “more autonomy”.

It is controlled autonomy.
The companies that adopt AI successfully will not be the ones that hand over their operations blindly.

They will be the ones that build the right layer between models, data, workflows and people.

A chatbot answers.
A Workling operates.

content:
AI is brilliant in the middle. You're needed at the edges. 🧭
A note for every young Forward Deployed Engineer whose only teammate is an AI model 👇
I watched Claude's "Delegation and the builder's toolkit" this week. One idea stuck with me: the hard part was never getting AI to write code. It's knowing what code you want written.
The video breaks a build into six capabilities. Look at where AI sits on each:
❤️ Empathy: what does the user actually need? → Human
🎨 Design: what should we build, and why? → Human (AI offers options)
🏗️ Architecture: how does it fit together? → Human + AI
⚙️ Implementation: writing the code → AI's strongest zone. Delegate hard.
⚖️ Judgment: is it good? Would you put your name on it? → Human
🚀 Shipping: real users, real feedback → Human
See the shape? AI dominates the middle. The edges are where the human work lives, and where the value is.
The example that landed for me: AI can't sit beside a clinic receptionist and notice she checks her phone dozens of times a day because patients keep calling about wait times. That observation is the product. And it's 100% human.
Here's the trap for FDEs who only build with AI: when code is instant, empathy and design start to feel like overhead. So you skip them. You ship fast. And you solve the wrong problem beautifully. 🙈
What human oversight really means:
🔍 Get clear on who you're building for before you prompt
🎯 Define success and tests before implementation starts
🧐 Inspect AI output skeptically, not gratefully
🪪 Keep the judgment calls in your own hands
After 25 years of delivery, I'll put it simply: the faster AI makes implementation, the more your value shifts to everything around it.
The builders who thrive won't be the fastest prompters. They'll be the ones who can tell the difference between "code that runs and code that matters." 💡
FDEs and early-career engineers: which edge do you find yourself skipping most? 👇

content:
Early in my P&G career, our first reads of online share showed we were lagging offline share. That gap prompted real action.

A third dimension is worth noting now: AI share. Offline share and online share both measure whether a human encounters your brand somewhere, a shelf, a search page, a feed. AI share measures something different: whether an AI agent, acting on someone's behalf, discovers your brand, compares and recommends it, without the human visiting the brand site.

This feels urgent. Cloudflare's CEO confirmed AI and bot traffic passed human traffic on the open web in May 2026, a year earlier than he'd forecast, and the company expects non-human traffic to outnumber human traffic by 1,000x within five years. Accenture's research already found Oreo showing up in just 10% of AI chatbot cookie recommendations, unexpectedly low for such an iconic brand. A friend, Filippo Catalano  Chief Information and Digital Officer at Mondelēz, has a phrase for what this demands: brand as code, which he talked about at the Vienna Consumer Goods Forum.

Boston Consulting Group (BCG)'s Mark Abraham, Jessica Apotheker, Yotam Ariav, Lauren Wiener and Robert Derow published research this week that feels highly relevant and timely. Touchpoints before a purchase have gone from 5 a decade ago to over 15 today. A large CPG company that needed about 500 marketing assets a year may now need 5 to 6 million. Unit costs are changing too. A personalized product image that cost $4 two years ago costs four cents now.

Incumbents need to treat that jump from 500 to 5-6 million assets as a real cost threat, and use AI to bring those costs down while still driving growth. New entrants don't carry that legacy weight, and AI is making them naturally leaner and faster, the same way e-commerce lowered entry barriers before, just exponentially more so now. Poppi's version of this is almost hard to believe: a business doing hundreds of millions in revenue runs entire marketing functions, copywriting, research, optimization, on one person each.

Google and Shopify's Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) already lets an agent complete a purchase directly inside the conversation. It's been live since January inside Google AI Mode, the Gemini app, and Microsoft Copilot.

Do you know what your brand's AI share is? Article link in the comment.

content:
Everyone seems to have an AI agent now.

Agents that answer questions.
Agents that automate workflows.
Agents that analyze information.
Agents that supposedly “do the work for you.”

But there’s a question organizations should be asking before any of that:

Are we actually ready for AI?

Before deploying an AI agent into your business, someone should understand your environment.

How do your workflows actually operate?

Where does your data live?

Is that data structured, governed, and trustworthy?

Who has access to it?

What permissions will the AI inherit?

Maybe your receptionist can’t access the company’s financial data.

But can an AI agent they’re authorized to use access it?

That’s a very different question.

AI is an extraordinary tool. Used well, it can help people work faster, make better use of information, become more creative, automate repetitive work, and spend more time on things that require human judgment.

But AI doesn’t fix broken processes.

It doesn’t fix poor data governance.

It doesn’t fix excessive permissions.

It doesn’t create institutional knowledge that was never documented.

And it doesn’t replace the need for policies governing how AI should—and shouldn’t—be used.

In fact, introducing AI into an organization that hasn’t addressed those things can amplify the problems that already exist.

And now they can happen faster.

That’s why we believe AI implementation shouldn’t begin with:

“What agent can we deploy?”

It should begin with:

“Is the organization ready?”

Then:

“What business problem are we trying to solve?”

Only then should we determine where AI belongs.

Because just because you CAN put an AI agent into a workflow doesn’t mean you SHOULD.

AI readiness comes before AI implementation.

For the past few weeks I've been experimenting with Laya, an open-source decision model based on Jev, together with Microsoft Copilot Studio.

The problem is one most companies have. Every email, ticket, form or record has to be sorted: which team owns it, how urgent it is, whether it needs escalating. Usually that means either people doing it by hand, which is slow, or a big general-purpose LLM, which spends time and tokens on what is really one simple decision.

Laya takes a different approach. It isn't a chatbot. It's built to make one decision quickly, and it tells you how confident it is. When it isn't sure, we can make it hand the item to a person.

What I like most is that we can ensure that nothing is a black box. Every decision shows up as a tree, so you can see exactly why something went where it did. Change a business rule and the path updates live.

In the video I use customer emails as the example, but the same pattern works for support tickets, sales leads, forms, documents or any data you need classified quickly and consistently.

Instead of pulling out your phone, opening an app, taking a picture, and asking a question...

you just ask.

You're in a meeting.

You need to remember something from earlier.

You don't stop everything to search through your notes.

You ask your AI.

You're travelling somewhere you've never been.

You need information about what's around you.

You don't necessarily reach for your phone.

Your AI is already there.

That's a very different interaction model.

We're moving from:

"I have to go to AI."

to:

"AI is already with me."

And that distinction matters.

Because the biggest limitation of today's AI isn't always intelligence.

Sometimes it's friction.

You have to open it.

You have to type.

You have to explain the context.

You have to give it information.

But an AI that is present in your environment can potentially understand much more of the context around you.

What you're looking at.

Where you are.

What you're doing.

What you're asking about.

And eventually, what you're trying to accomplish.

That's when AI starts feeling less like a chatbot...

and more like an actual computing interface.

And Meta isn't the only company moving in this direction.

We're seeing the industry explore AI through glasses, voice, agents and other interfaces that don't require us to constantly stare at a screen.

The smartphone gave us computing everywhere.

AI might give us intelligence everywhere.

Of course, there are huge questions here.

Privacy.

Security.

Permissions.

Accuracy.

And how much of our everyday environment we actually want an AI to understand.

Those questions are going to matter just as much as the technology itself.

But as a developer, this is the part I'm excited to watch.

Because the next generation of AI products may not be another app sitting on your phone.

They may be the interface through which you interact with the world itself.

And honestly...

that feels much bigger than another chatbot.

Bit of an update: since May, I’ve been supporting Government Digital Service on Developer Experience and Cloud Platform UX research (UXR). 

I also recently took a training break to visit Vienna for uxcon vienna. One talk that stood out was from Anthropic’s Head of Design, who spoke about the changing role of the UX professional — to builder. She also urged that every UX pro in future needs to understand CI/CD tools and what engineers do in this context, this last point was the more relevant for my current contract.

For those that attended her workshop, I was interested to hear that Anthropic might not kickstart their designs in Claude, still relying on Figma, but then supposedly in later design stages use Claude Design embedded in Slack.

The missed opportunity for me, however, was the Anthropic speaker’s response to a question on the environmental impact of AI: treating it as just another of the ‘many problems we have to deal with’. With great AI data centre usage — especially in the era of peak water — comes great responsibility. But it seems Anthropic aren’t looking to be the super eco hero of our times.

Moving onto Nielsen Norman Group, Maria Rosala gave me a lot of hope. Her polished sampling of prose from J.L Borges to T.S. Eliot helped illuminate our understanding of the researcher in the age of AI, using Eliot’s quote:

‘Where is the wisdom we have lost in knowledge? Where is the knowledge we have lost in information?’
Her overall message was that the human UXR is still best placed to apply collectively the rigour and wisdom needed for better design decisions.

Elizabeth Churchill’s charting of AI from a historical HCI lens also stood out. Her take on AI, from the Dartmouth College days in the 1950s, and talked about its predominantly WEIRD base (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic), this highlighted for me how LLM ecosystems carry ethnocentric bias and limitations in types of intelligence. I mean, just ask Gemini AI if it’s WEIRD and see the response!

Her call for UXR, and particularly ethnographers, to play an active role in understanding the application and impact of multi-agent AI systems — or ‘swarm AI’, as she referred to it — this along with Michael Kibedi talk on Voice UX gaps in reading regional accents, working class forms of Spoken English gave me renewed hope that my anthropology degree might come in use again.

content:
93.8% F1. That's my retrieval benchmark on my AI receptionist's knowledge base, and I spent more time writing down what it doesn't measure than getting the number itself.

It doesn't tell you whether the written answer is any good. It doesn't tell you whether the agent picks the right tool. And it doesn't tell you the production embedder is fine, because I ran a deterministic stub offline to keep the test reproducible.

Eighteen queries. Fifteen chunks. A dental clinic. Precision 88.2%, recall 100%, similarity threshold 0.35.

What it actually guards is the retrieval policy — the similarity floor, the top-k cut, vector versus keyword — so that when I change the pipeline next month I find out immediately, instead of finding out from a customer.

Here's why I bothered. Almost everyone selling you an AI feature will show you a number. Almost none of them will tell you what they left out of it. If a vendor hands you 99% accuracy and won't answer three questions — what was the test set, who wrote it, what does it exclude — then that number isn't a measurement, it's decoration.

If you're in legal, compliance, support or research, where an answer without a source is worse than no answer at all, those are the exclusions you should be asking about. Not the headline.

The harness is public: djaouad.is-a.dev — the retrieval policy, the benchmark, and four live systems behind it.

We're moving from:
“Which AI should I use?”
to:
“Which AI should handle this job?”
Big difference.
And probably a much bigger business opportunity.
Would you rather have one excellent AI...
or one workspace that knows when to use several?

Relying on a single AI model for high-stakes decisions is like hiring one advisor and forbidding them from checking their work. 

Every major LLM has blind spots. ChatGPT delivers razor-sharp structure, Claude handles nuanced reasoning, Gemini synthesizes deep context, and specialized open-source models excel at raw code. Yet most teams are still copy-pasting prompts back and forth across a dozen open browser tabs.
Multi-model workspaces (like Multi) are replacing single-chatbot silos:

1. Side-by-Side Comparison: Run one prompt across multiple models simultaneously to evaluate factual accuracy, tone, and logic instantly.
2. Model Councils: Let a panel of models draft, critique, and cross-check each other before a judge model synthesizes the strongest answer.
3. Smart Model Routing: Automatically pair specific tasks—coding, deep research, or quick summaries—with the exact model best suited for the job.

The operational reality from active power users:
- Zero vendor lock-in means you immediately adopt frontier releases as labs leapfrog each other.
- Managing model selection, API key setups, and multi-model councils carries a higher initial learning curve than a single prompt box.
-  Built-in quality assurance catches hallucinatory blind spots before work touches production.

If your daily output requires high-accuracy research, code, or strategic copywriting, single-model workflows are quickly becoming an operational bottleneck.

content:
"Know your worth" is terrible pricing advice. Your worth is irrelevant until you understand what the outcome is worth to a client.

What's one new customer worth to them? That number sets your ceiling.

What's delivery costs for you? That number sets your floor.

Price somewhere in between.

Here's how we determine our pricing so it makes sense for both parties:

We see people get it wrong both ways.

They charge $500 for something worth tens of thousands to the client.

Or they sell something for $2,500...

Then realise it costs $2,000 to deliver.

TONS of work for $500.

Five things fix this:

>Value
>Scope
>Cost
>Risk
>Price

In that order.

1: Value

Before you think about price, ask the client:

What's one customer worth to you?
What's your gross profit per deal?
How often do customers buy?
How long do they stay?

One of our clients pitched a water filtration company.
One new customer = $5,000/month.
Say they stay 12 months.
That's a $60,000 customer.
Pitch a lead gen system at $2,500/month.
One extra customer & it pays for itself twice over.

Now work the funnel backwards:

100 leads.
30% book -> 30 calls.
70% show -> 21 calls.
5 close.
At $60,000 each & a 60% margin...
That's $36,000 profit per customer.
$180,000 across all 5.

This can go both ways.

Another client quoted a small trucking company $3,900 for a website...crickets.

Their loads come through elsewhere.
The website just proves they exist.
So low value=low price ceiling.

2: Scope

"AI receptionist" isn't a project.
 It's a category.

1 phone number or 8 locations?
1 department or 6?
1 language or 3?
Books appointments? Syncs to the CRM? Works after hours?

Every answer is a different scope.

Step 3: Cost

Never sell it & figure out delivery later.
Take the scope to your tech VA or implementation partner, or just yourself.

Before the proposal goes out.
Ask: "What will this take to build?"

An example breakdown could be:

Integration: $1,200
Software & setup: $250
Internal management: $300
Testing & contingency: $250

That's $2,000 before you've made a dollar.

Sell it for $2,500?
$500 left. Before overhead, support & acquisition costs.

Revenue isn't profit!

A $3,000/month client costing $1,800/month to fulfil...

That's not a $3,000 client.
That's $1,200 gross profit.

Watch the usage costs.
Voice minutes.
SMS.
API calls.
Hosting.

Client's usage doubles -> your costs double.

These are things to factor into your price.

Step 4: Risk.

Obscure systems to connect?
CRM a total mess?
Scope still vague?
Compliance issues?
Want it live next Tuesday?

Ambiguity is EXPENSIVE.

More uncertainty means you need one of three things:

More:

- Margin
- Scope
- Higher price

Often the smartest move is a smaller phase 1.
Prove it works.
Learn their business.
Then expand.

Step 5: Price.

Your costs set the floor.
Their value sets the ceiling.
Your price lives somewhere in between.

Find the spot that's good for both sides.

content:
Today I had the chance to attend Fintech Moldova Conference 2026 representing CLOWD9 | Certified B Corp™ 

A lot of interesting discussions around AI, cloud, Open Finance and the future of payments, but one idea stood out to me more than anything else:

AI in banking doesn't start with AI.

It starts with data.

We talk a lot about AI agents, automation and the future of payments. But underneath all of that, the foundations still matter.

A few things that stuck with me:

→ Data is the first layer

You can't meaningfully implement AI in banking or payments without having the right data, structure and access to it first

AI is only as useful as the infrastructure underneath it

→ Cloud and payments increasingly go hand in hand

Modern financial products require infrastructure that can scale quickly, process huge amounts of data and support increasingly intelligent services

And AI is becoming part of that infrastructure.

One example shared around Amazon was particularly interesting: customers using Amazon's AI shopping assistant are 60%+ more likely to complete a purchase

That's a huge reminder that AI becomes interesting when it starts changing actual business metrics

Not when we add a chatbot because everyone else has one

→ AI governance will become as important as AI capability

Banks can't simply deploy models and hope for the best

Who controls the data?
How do you explain decisions?
How do you manage risk?
Who is accountable when an AI agent starts taking actions?

The more autonomous financial systems become, the more important these questions get.

→ Agentic payments are getting closer

We're moving from AI helping users understand something to AI potentially being able to initiate and manage actions on their behalf

That changes the role of payments infrastructure significantly.

→ Open Banking is moving from infrastructure to actual use cases

Faster lending decisions, cleaner AML processes, better data enrichment and more personalized financial experiences are where the value starts becoming visible

→ Payments are becoming an interoperability problem

Instant payments, cross-border payments, Open Finance, cards and new payment rails increasingly need to work together rather than exist as isolated ecosystems.

My biggest reflection after the conference:

AI might be the visible layer of the next generation of financial services, but data, cloud infrastructure, governance and payments rails are what will actually make it possible.

Build those foundations well, and AI becomes powerful.

Skip them, and AI is mostly a demo.

Great to represent CLOWD9 | Certified B Corp™  and be part of the conversation around where banking and payments are heading next

content:
OpenAI's DevDay was yesterday. By their own recap it carried more than 20 announcements across agents, models, developer tools and the ChatGPT surface. I read the full list looking for video generation.

There is none. Not one item.

Because Sora is already gone. The web and app experiences were discontinued in April, the API was discontinued on September 24, five days ago, and OpenAI's deprecation page lists no replacement for it.

Here is why that should matter to anyone running a content operation, and not just to people who liked Sora.

The model layer is the least durable layer in the stack. A generator you build your weekly process around can be retired on a Tuesday, and you will not get a migration path, because the replacement column is empty.

The company with the most resources in artificial intelligence held its largest event of the year and had nothing to say about the category. That is not a product having a bad quarter. That is a direction.

So the question worth asking about your own content business is simple. If your generator disappeared tomorrow, what would you still have?

I built my product with one tool and no budget, because paying for five separate subscriptions was never going to happen. And I am not going to pretend it is immune to this. Nothing built on someone else's generator is.

But there is a real distinction between the parts of the flow that are mine and the part that is rented. The posting accounts are mine. The content calendar is mine. The avatar and the voice profile are mine. The generation model is rented.

If a model gets swapped, that costs me a generator. It does not cost me the audience, the schedule, the attribution or the story.

Rent the model. Own the accounts. That is the part of this I would put in a budget line.

#contentstrategy #solopreneur #creatoreconomy

content:
Your dryer shows "tE1". The paper manual is long gone. A chatbot gives you a confident answer, but is it about YOUR machine?

I built FixIt for the Build, Ship, Shape: Amazon Developer Hackathon: an open-source MCP server, built for Alexa+, that answers appliance error codes and symptoms from the real manufacturer manual and cites the page. If the manual doesn't say, FixIt says so.

The design rule: no model runs inside any tool. All the AI work happens offline. Every live answer is a fast, testable lookup. The model presents, the tool decides.

What I learned building it:

→ An empty field is not a fact. The assistant once called an empty warning list "safe." Now it says "the manual doesn't list one."

→ Some PDFs lie quietly. Two of my seven manuals extracted as plausible-looking garbage, shifted by a constant character offset. Nothing errored. The fix is now an open-source library: pdf-encoding-repair, on PyPI.

→ Publish the weak numbers too. 62 of 63 cases fully grounded in one eval run. But my keyword symptom matcher only got 4 of 10 on phrasings it hadn't been tuned for. Both are in the repo.

→ Read the billing page. Claude on Bedrock is sold through AWS Marketplace, so my hackathon credit didn't cover it. A $12 lesson, now a friction-log entry.

It runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (Runtime and Memory) with CloudWatch alarms. One honest caveat: Alexa+ developer tools aren't available to hackathon participants, so the demo uses a clearly labelled simulated Alexa+ client.

If you're building AI agents or MCP servers and need them right rather than just fluent, send me a DM.

content:
Your chatbot is a dangerous sycophant and you don’t know it. 

We’re all cautious about AI hallucinations. But we may be far less guarded when Claude, Grok, Gemini or ChatGPT agrees with us or WORSE compliments our ideas. That could be more dangerous than it seems. Here’s why.

Eugene Torres, an accountant with no history of mental illness, began using a chatbot for everyday office tasks. Within weeks, he believed he was living in a false universe. Following the chatbot’s advice, he increased his ketamine use and cut off his family. Another user, Allan Brooks, became convinced he’d made a world-changing mathematical discovery. Strikingly, both eventually suspected the chatbot was just telling them what they wanted to hear, and kept spiraling anyway.

They’re not isolated cases. Nearly 300 have been documented, and serious ones have been linked to at least 14 deaths and 5 wrongful-death lawsuits against AI companies.

Researchers call this “delusional spiraling,” and two recent studies help explain it.

There is a pattern in real conversations!
Stanford researchers analyzed 19 real human–chatbot transcripts. Again and again, a person shared an unusual, grandiose or paranoid idea, and the chatbot affirmed it, encouraged it and sometimes helped build on it. It did all this with warm, almost human reassurance, and without the pushback a friend or therapist would give.

Why even rational people are vulnerable? 
Researchers at MIT and the University of Washington modeled a perfectly logical user talking to a chatbot that tends to validate them. Even this idealized thinker could be pulled into false beliefs. They also tested two common fixes:
• Forcing the bot to state only true facts reduced the risk, but didn’t remove it. Selectively chosen truths are enough to mislead.
• Warning users about sycophancy also reduced the risk a lot, but not to zero.

What the researchers recommend :
• Developers should test models for their tendency to fuel delusional spirals, and tackle sycophancy directly, not just hallucinations.
• Policymakers could treat this as a public-health issue, with standards for flagging sensitive conversations and clear crisis-escalation rules.

So, next time your favourite AI tells you you’re a genius, that’s exactly the moment to go looking for someone who might tell you you’re wrong.

content:
AI is slowly leaving the screen.

And I don't think most people have realized how big that shift could be.

Think about how we use AI today.

You have a question.

You open ChatGPT.

You type.

You get an answer.

You want something scheduled.

You ask your AI assistant.

You want something researched.

You open an app.

There is always a screen between you and the AI.

But what happens when that screen starts disappearing?

That's what caught my attention about Meta's latest announcements.

At Connect 2026, Meta introduced Muse, its personal AI agent, and announced that Muse is coming to its AI glasses.

And this is where things get interesting.

Imagine you're walking down the street.

You see something you don't recognize.

Instead of pulling out your phone, opening an app, taking a picture, and asking a question...

you just ask.

You're in a meeting.

You need to remember something from earlier.

You don't stop everything to search through your notes.

You ask your AI.

You're travelling somewhere you've never been.

You need information about what's around you.

You don't necessarily reach for your phone.

Your AI is already there.

That's a very different interaction model.

We're moving from:

"I have to go to AI."

to:

"AI is already with me."

And that distinction matters.

Because the biggest limitation of today's AI isn't always intelligence.

Sometimes it's friction.

You have to open it.

You have to type.

You have to explain the context.

You have to give it information.

But an AI that is present in your environment can potentially understand much more of the context around you.

What you're looking at.

Where you are.

What you're doing.

What you're asking about.

And eventually, what you're trying to accomplish.

That's when AI starts feeling less like a chatbot...

and more like an actual computing interface.

And Meta isn't the only company moving in this direction.

We're seeing the industry explore AI through glasses, voice, agents and other interfaces that don't require us to constantly stare at a screen.

The smartphone gave us computing everywhere.

AI might give us intelligence everywhere.

Of course, there are huge questions here.

Privacy.

Security.

Permissions.

Accuracy.

And how much of our everyday environment we actually want an AI to understand.

Those questions are going to matter just as much as the technology itself.

But as a developer, this is the part I'm excited to watch.

Because the next generation of AI products may not be another app sitting on your phone.

They may be the interface through which you interact with the world itself.

And honestly...

that feels much bigger than another chatbot.

content:
Caught the Manus 2.0 announcement video today, and whether or not you use their platform, the product shift they're pitching is interesting to watch.

Most early agent tools focused on an all-or-nothing model: you type a prompt, the agent works behind the scenes, and it hands you a finished output in a closed sandbox. The problem with that approach has always been control. The moment you want to change one detail, re-prompting often scrambles the rest of the work.

Looking at their 2.0 breakdown, the focus seems to be shifting toward giving users manual control back:

• Moving from one-shot outputs to editable workspaces. Instead of just exporting a locked video or prototype, they're introducing multi-track timelines and inspectors so creators can manually tweak audio, swap footage, or adjust code.

• Bridging cloud sandboxes with local workflows. Agents are starting to interact with local files and persistent servers rather than staying trapped inside a single browser tab.

• Tackling the "first cut" rather than the whole finish line. The pitch is about letting AI generate the rough 80% foundation, while leaving the final 20% of craft, polish, and tuning to the user.

As these platforms mature, the competition seems less about who has the cleverest chatbot and more about who builds the best hybrid workspace—combining fast generative scaffolding with deterministic, granular controls.

For developers and designers: When you see tools like this, do you prefer full autonomy from an agent, or do you always want a timeline and inspector to fine-tune the output yourself?

content: 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗙𝗥𝗢𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗡𝗗 𝗜𝗦 𝗖𝗛𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗜𝗡𝗚 🚀The biggest shift in frontend isnt a new JS framework. Its not a new state-management library or a faster build tool. The real shift? 𝗔𝗜 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝘄𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘂𝘀𝗲 software.And this time, it isnt just a trend developers are experimenting with—AI is already embedded in everyday engineering.Developers use AI to:🔹 Generate components🔹 Understand codebases🔹 Debug complex issues🔹 Write test suites🔹 Refactor code🔹 Build features fasterBut developer productivity is *only half the story.*───𝗔𝗜 𝗜𝗦 𝗖𝗛𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗨𝗦𝗘𝗥 𝗘𝗫𝗣𝗘𝗥𝗜𝗘𝗡𝗖𝗘 𝗧𝗢𝗢 💡For years, we interacted with applications through rigid, predefined flows:𝗖𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗸 ➔ 𝗡𝗮𝘃𝗶𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗲 ➔ 𝗙𝗶𝗹𝗹 ➔ 𝗦𝘂𝗯𝗺𝗶𝘁AI introduces a completely new possibility:𝗗𝗲𝘀𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗯𝗲 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘄𝗮𝗻𝘁 ➔ 𝗟𝗲𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 intent.Instead of navigating through multiple screens or applying several filters, users can increasingly describe the outcome theyre looking for.*But this doesnt mean every application needs a generic chatbot.*The interesting future isnt **chat replacing UI**. Its **AI and traditional UI working together in harmony:**👉 Sometimes a simple button is still the best interface.👉 Sometimes its a structured form, a table, or a dashboard.👉 Sometimes its a conversational prompt.The frontend is becoming smart enough to adapt and choose the right interaction for the situation.───𝗦𝗢 𝗪𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗛𝗔𝗣𝗣𝗘𝗡𝗦 𝗧𝗢 𝗙𝗥𝗢𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗡𝗗 𝗗𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗟𝗢𝗣𝗘𝗥𝗦? 🛠️The fundamentals arent going away.HTML, CSS, JavaScript, TypeScript, React, accessibility, performance, architecture, and design systems still matter deeply.But the boundaries of frontend engineering are expanding rapidly.Frontend developers increasingly need to master:⚡ AI APIs amp; integration⚡ Real-time streaming responses⚡ Structured outputs amp; schema validation⚡ Autonomous agents amp; context systems⚡ AI-driven user experiencesAs AI makes writing code easier, **engineering judgment becomes infinitely more valuable.**Generating code is becoming trivial. Knowing *what to build*, *why to build it*, and *how it should behave* remains the real challenge.───𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗟 𝗦𝗛𝗜𝗙𝗧 ⚡Perhaps the biggest change isnt that AI can generate frontend code.Its that the fundamental relationship between **users**, **applications**, and **developers** is changing:1️⃣ **Developers** use AI to build applications faster.2️⃣ **Applications** use AI to understand user intent.3️⃣ **Users** use AI to interact with applications naturally.The frontend sits right in the middle of all three.Thats why were entering one of the most interesting, high-impact phases of frontend development yet.**The frontend isnt disappearing. Its evolving.** 🔥#FrontendDevelopment #AIinTech #WebDevelopment

content:
Hands-On AI Development with Python by Author Vivian Aranha is an excellent resource for any developer or AI novice to uncover the basics of AI model building, training, testing, and evaluation. I believe in the philosophy of learning by doing and this resource does just that. To maximize the most from this book, it’s best to install Python 3.8 or higher and used Jupyter Notebook or your preferred IDE. For each covered topic, the author removes the ambiguity dives right into practical cases.

There are seven chapters in this book, six of which go into theory and practical examples. Aranha makes no assumption that you know Python, but provides a review of syntax, logic, flows and libraries in Chapter 1. Chapter 2 dives into Machine Learning and Classification Models which covers Supervised vs Unsupervised Learning for models. He mainly focuses on supervised learning which uses linear and logistic regression models to train on real sample data from Kaggle, IMDB, image files, text files, speech files and others. He also demonstrates for the reader how to evaluate the efficacy of the model using the Mean Squared Error and R-Squared Error and plot how well a model predicts values versus the actual values. Aranha provides many examples throughout the book how to effectively install needed libraries, import the libraries, define functions, call functions, load datasets, split and test datasets and evaluate models using a Confusion matrix. Chapter 4 shows the reader how to build and actually deploy an AI model as a web service.

There are a several examples to follow along to, some of which determine if an email is a spam risk, building a calculator, predicting car values, predicting house values, probability of diabetes, chatbots and many others. Chapter 6 takes more of an advanced turn toward Deep learning, Natural Language Processing, Neural Network Models and introduces Bayes Classifiers and explains testing these models and weights with Forward and Backward Pass Propagation for evaluation and model correction. One example that resonated with me was the Tic-Tac-Toe game which is similar to what I used in my senior project in college using C++. For this example, Aranha provides explanations and coding for each phase of the game using a MiniMax algorithm to check and calculate the best probability required to beat human interaction by propagating to negative or positive infinity looking at all possibilities on the board using recursive calls in its' simulation before a move is made. It's amazing that Python does this using pre-built mathematical functions as opposed to all the manual stuff I placed into C++ decades ago.

A lot of ground is covered in this smaller than the typical AI resource, but this is a must have for developers who are new to AI and want the hands-on experience. Great book to add to your collection. 
Thanks to Packt Shruthi Shetty Vivian Aranha for an incredible work. Find it at https://packt.link/pZ2C5.

content:
LangChain is not the thing you need to learn.
The architecture behind it is.

I've interviewed people who could explain:
• Chains
• Agents
• Memory
• Retrievers
• Tools

But when I asked:
"How does a user query actually travel through a RAG application?"
The answers got vague.
That's the problem.

Many developers memorize LangChain components.
Few understand how they work together.

A production AI application is not:
Prompt → LLM → Done
It's usually:
Document Loader
→ Text Splitter
→ Embeddings
→ Vector Store
→ Retriever
→ Prompt
→ Model
→ Output Parser
→ Memory
→ Monitoring

Every component exists for a reason.
Bad chunking?
Retrieval quality drops.
Wrong embedding model?
Relevant documents disappear.
No memory?
Your chatbot forgets everything.
No observability?
Good luck debugging production issues.

The biggest advantage of learning LangChain isn't the framework itself.
It's learning the architecture of modern AI applications.

Because once you understand:
→ Retrieval
→ Context Management
→ Tool Calling
→ State Management
→ Agent Workflows

You can build the same systems with any framework.
LangChain.
LangGraph.
LlamaIndex.
DSPy.
Or your own code.
Frameworks change.
Architecture stays.

This carousel is one of the best visual breakdowns of how all LangChain components fit together into a real RAG application.

Save it.
You'll come back to it more than once.

content:
That next major step wasn’t just about speed, it was about pushing what the native pipeline could actually compute. With the Kotlin foundation set, I started building the tools I always wanted in a mobile editor.

Standard RGB curves are fine, but they inherently link brightness to saturation. To fix this, I Introduced a CIELAB (CIE L*a*b*) processing pipeline using native OpenGL. By mathematically separating Lightness from the color channels, users can now adjust shadow and highlight contrast without artificially inflating or shifting the underlying hues.

I took the same physics-based approach to texture. Instead of using heavy, static image overlays for film grain, I added a procedural generator directly into the shader. It combines Simplex Noise to simulate organic clumping with Hash Noise for pixel-level grit. It even mimics real silver-halide film by naturally peaking in the mid tones and rolling off in extreme shadows and highlights.

But the most ambitious addition was Lens Blur.

I didn’t want a cheap, flat blur. I wanted real optical depth.

I integrated a depth-estimation engine that reads actual image segmentation maps (depth maps & blur maps). It doesn’t just look for faces, the model detects and isolates any subject (humans, animals, objects, you name it). Instead of an arbitrary "blur amount" slider, the engine is controlled by standard photographic f-stops, mapping everything from a creamy f/1.2 down to a sharp f/22 to exact optical blur radii with a proper depth of field transition. I pushed the rendering pipeline to support custom iris shapes (like pentagons and hexagons), anamorphic stretch, subject protection, and face-detection autofocus.

Processing this level of optical simulation on a phone requires serious computational power, relying heavily on modern AGSL hardware support; but the result is an authentic subject-background separation that actually feels like it was shot on a fast, physical lens.

Every one of these features broke the architecture in new ways, forcing me to rethink rendering loops and memory management. But that’s the reality of building Luttify: the product pushes the architecture, and the architecture enables the product.

A quick note on how this actually gets built: I am not an expert in writing shaders or some heavy mathematical logics. To get these complex OpenGL pipelines working, I honestly relied a lot on the free versions of AI chatbots to refine, debug, and improve the shader code. That, alongside deep dives into countless open-source repos and developer forums, was absolutely essential to bringing these features to life.

Luttify is still in beta, but it has already grown far beyond what I originally imagined when it was just a simple LUT tool. I’m looking forward to seeing where it goes next.

content:
🚀 A project I’ve been building while exploring Agentic AI — meet Syntra!

I’ve been experimenting with AI agents lately, and I wanted to build something beyond a chatbot that simply takes a prompt and generates a response.

So I built Syntra — an AI Engineering Agent designed to understand software tasks, work with GitHub repositories, understand project context, use tools, and help move a task towards implementation.

The idea was simple:

What if an AI agent could actually work on a software project instead of just telling you how to build it?

The most interesting part for me was understanding how different AI components fit together into one Agentic AI architecture.

🧠 The architecture behind Syntra

User Request → Context Retrieval → Reasoning → Planning → Tool Selection → Execution → Validation → Result

📚 RAG & Project Context
An agent needs to understand the project it is working with. RAG allows Syntra to retrieve relevant project information instead of relying only on the LLM's general knowledge.

🔹 Chunking & Embeddings
Project files can be broken into meaningful chunks and converted into vector embeddings that capture their semantic meaning.

🗄️ Vector Database & Semantic Search
These embeddings can be stored and searched to retrieve the most relevant context for a developer's request.

🧠 LLM & Agent Orchestration
The LLM uses the retrieved context to reason about the request, break it into tasks and decide what should happen next.

🔧 Tool Calling
The agent can move beyond generating text and interact with capabilities such as GitHub, project files, APIs and other tools.

⚙️ Execution & Validation
The planned task can then move towards execution, followed by validation and result tracking.

So instead of:

Prompt → LLM → Response

the goal becomes:

Understand → Retrieve → Reason → Plan → Use Tools → Execute → Validate

💡 What I learned

Building Syntra showed me that Agentic AI is much more than choosing an LLM.

A lot of the engineering happens around the model — context management, RAG, embeddings, vector search, tools, APIs, databases and execution.

Working on Syntra has given me hands-on experience with:

🔹 Agentic AI & LLMs
🔹 RAG & Semantic Search
🔹 Vector Embeddings & Vector Databases
🔹 Tool Calling & Agent Orchestration
🔹 GitHub APIs
🔹 FastAPI, React & TypeScript
🔹 PostgreSQL & JWT Authentication

Syntra is still a work in progress, and I’m looking forward to exploring better codebase understanding, memory, retrieval and more reliable autonomous execution.

How I'm preparing to win with SEO in 2027 (and how you can too)

Simple steps that you can start doing today.

A few months ago, one of my best-ranking posts lost a big chunk of its traffic. 

Nothing was wrong with it. It was a "what is X" guide that still sat on page one.

The problem was that Google now answers that question before anyone clicks.

I'm not the only one seeing it. A randomized field experiment found AI Overviews cut organic clicks by 38% on queries where they appear, and zero-click searches jumped from 54% to 72%. 

Pew Research found that people click organic results only 8% of the time when an AI Overview shows up, versus 15% without one. 

And on informational queries, Seer Interactive saw organic CTR fall 61%, from 1.76% to 0.61%.  (Study Confirms Google AI Overviews Cut Organic Clicks 38% +2)

 As I'm watching all this happening and where the real conversion are going forward,and basically it changed how I plan content. 

Old SEO isn't dead. 
Generic content is.

Here's what I'm doing:
1. Cutting the commodity stuff.
If a chatbot can answer it in two seconds, it's not a strategy. I'm auditing my pages and keeping only the topics where my own experience adds something.

2. Going after bottom-of-funnel searches.
People comparing tools or services are still clicking through to websites. So I'm writing more "X vs Y" and "best for" pages.

3. Putting my own proof in everything.
My tests, my screenshots, my results. A committee can't fake that, and neither can AI.

4. Making every article do more than one job.
One piece now becomes SEO traffic, social posts, sales material, and a YouTube video.

5. Building an original data asset.
A survey or trend page that journalists and AI tools actually want to cite. 

This matters because brands cited inside an AI summary got 35% higher organic CTR than brands that ranked at the same level but weren't cited.  (mersel)

If you want to start this week, here's how:

→ Pick your 5 weakest "definition" pages and decide whether to rewrite them with real experience or retire them.

→ Write one comparison post for a decision your customers actually face.

→ Before you publish anything, ask yourself: "What can only I say here?"

→ Run one tiny data project, even a 10-question survey of your audience.
You don't need a bigger team. 

You need a sharper point of view.

🙋Has AI search hit your traffic yet? Which of these five would you start with? 

Tell me in the comments 👇

As a first-year BTech student, I recently attended a 3-day bootcamp organized by KRIVA Machine Learning Society, where I learned about AI, machine learning concepts, and how these technologies can be applied to build practical projects.

Inspired by what I learned during the bootcamp, I worked on my first end-to-end AI project — AI Navigator, a beginner-friendly chatbot designed to help users discover the right AI tools for their needs.

💡 The idea is simple:

There are hundreds of AI tools available today, and beginners often don't know which one to use for a particular task.

AI Navigator lets users describe what they want to accomplish in natural language and then recommends relevant AI tools.

⚙️ How it works:

• User enters a natural-language query
• FastAPI processes the request
• Sentence Transformers generate embeddings using all-MiniLM-L6-v2
• Cosine similarity performs semantic search
• The system identifies relevant AI tools from a JSON knowledge base
• Groq-powered AI generates a beginner-friendly response
• Recommended tools are displayed with descriptions, use cases, limitations, and website links

• Python

content:
Something caught my attention recently. Amazon told Meta's new AI agent, Muse, to stay out.
Muse isn't just another chatbot. It can browse, make bookings, fill forms and take actions on your behalf.
Then Amazon blocked it from shopping on Amazon. 
Interestingly, Shopify took the opposite approach and welcomed it. I've been thinking about why, because in my view this is an early sign of a much bigger shift in the AI economy.

When someone else's agent sits between you and your customer, the conversation, comparison and increasingly the decision move towards the agent. 
The merchant risks becoming the fulfilment layer at the end of someone else's choice.
If you think carefully the old battle was for the click.The new battle could be for the decision.
And the economics are starting to follow.
Stripe recently agreed to acquire OpenRouter — a gateway to 400+ AI models. Stripe already sits in payments and billing, while its Link wallet enables purchases through Muse.
So basically it's about Model routing → usage → agent checkout → payments.
Stripe doesn't need to predict which model wins. It is positioning itself around the economic activity those models create.

Thats what I have started thinking of as the "AI Toll Booth". 

And it isn't just Stripe.
Visa and Mastercard are building trust and payment rails for agents. Shopify is opening merchant infrastructure to AI. Walmart is bringing its own commerce experience into ChatGPT.

Different companies. Different layers.

But the direction of travel looks increasingly clear:
AI is moving from answering to deciding to acting then transacting.
For enterprises, that creates some practical questions:
→ Are our products and services discoverable by agents, not just humans?
→ How will we identify an agent, who it represents and what it is authorised to do?→ Who decides which external agents can access or transact with our business?
→ Where are we becoming dependent on someone else's AI control point?

My view isn't that every enterprise should build its own toll booth.Instead, decide deliberately:
What should we OWN?
What should we OPEN?
What are we comfortable RENTING?
And where we depend on someone else's AI layer, preserve the ability to route around it.
Optionality could become one of the most important architectural principles of the AI economy.

And there is a bigger strategic question:
If AI agents become the new interface to your customers, will your business still own the customer relationship? What happens when your next customer doesn't search Google, visit your website or speak to sales — but simply asks an AI agent what to buy?

AI strategy is moving beyond model strategy.
AI architecture is becoming business-model architecture.

In my opinion, 
The AI race is moving from model capability to control of the value chain.
The question is no longer just what AI can do — but who owns the layer through which it acts.

content:
Defaulting to an AI chatbot on a website confuses understanding a customer's intent with helping a customer solve a problem.

Beyond being another channel for accessing existing information, AI's real strength should be in answering: What is the best interaction for this intent?

Digital channel teams know they need to do something with AI, and the natural first step is to explore chat as a capability on the website. That makes sense at first. It forces teams to get their content in order, which supports both GEO and retrieval through their own LLM. The vendors and models are well known. Customers understand ChatGPT. Throwing a bubble in the bottom-right corner feels like an easy win.

Natural language is better at capturing intent and complex queries, particularly across multiple turns. But we need to separate capturing intent from solving the problem.

The most efficient next step may not be displaying an FAQ-like answer or completing a task through a series of back-and-forth questions.

In the luxury jet space, a question like, “I regularly need to fly a group of 12 from Vancouver to Tokyo” is better routed to a compare-and-configure tool with that context passed through—not an endless chat experience, or, forbid, a dump of flight-distance and seating specs.

Separating intent from interface also opens up more than routing to existing tools. It creates room for newer design paradigms like Generative UI, where an interface can be created on the fly for a specific problem, and eventually for agent-to-agent interactions where my agent can interact directly with a brand’s agent.

So the architecture should look more like:

Enterprise knowledge + services  
↓  
Intelligence / orchestration layer  
↓  
Human interfaces: browse, search, answers, GenUI, chat, forms, tools  
Machine interfaces: APIs, MCP, agent protocols

We shouldn’t just be bolting chat onto existing websites. AI is an opportunity to rethink the product, the customer journey, and how digital channels actually help people solve problems.

If natural language helps us understand what someone is trying to do, the next question is: what is the best way to help them do it?

content:
The 49ERS, Meta Muse and the Winners/Losers 

Deciding to go to the 49ers game against the Arizona Cardinals last Sunday sparked a real-world test of Meta Muse. Because the decision was made just a day before, downloading Muse and asking it to find the cheapest 49ers tickets under $150 served as a fascinating look into how agentic workflows operate under the hood. Watching an AI agent spin up tools to search, compare, and monitor prices raises a bigger question: What kind of events and computing resources are actually required to power an agentic task and who are the winners and losers?

The key shift here is a shift to per user model. Traditional chatbots consume resources dynamically only when a prompt is entered. In contrast, agentic platforms like Meta Muse open a secure VM (virtual machine) for each user to keep track of background tasks, run recurring loops, and manage isolated actions. As the flow below indicates, it has to 

Decide and Plan- which websites to look at for those tickets. Needs more GPU's
Memorize- Hold the context and lot of what the model processes. Seat numbers, ticket prices, individual preferences etc. Needs more memory.
Act- Open the website, fill user details and book. CPUs help carry that out.

This architectural shift has major ripple effects across the technology stack:

I just read a story about a federal park ranger who said visitors are showing up with AI-generated itineraries containing imaginary campsites and routes that require rowing upstream where it isn’t possible.

Some of them still believe their chosen AI chatbot even after a real, living, human forest ranger points out the errors on a map. 

That should give anyone automating their business with AI pause.

An AI-generated strategy, marketing plan, or website mockup can be just as convincing. So can a customer email, a sales follow-up, or a recommendation about where to invest your budget.

Outputs can look and sound completely convincing even when the facts, assumptions, or logic are wrong.

And when you automate mass communications, mistakes can reach hundreds of clients or prospects before anyone catches them.

My entire team and I use AI extensively, and it's built into our products at Snappy Kraken. But our approach to keeping a “human in the loop” means more than having someone skim outputs and click approve.

The people using AI need enough judgment to challenge strategy, verify claims, understand clients, recognize quality, and catch promises the business can’t keep.

Review also needs to happen before workflows go live. Who defines the objective? What information and data can the AI rely on? Which decisions require approval? When does it hand the conversation to a person?

Those are leadership decisions, and leaders remain accountable for them.

AI can help us do more, but it doesn’t remove the need for judgment. Firms that treat it as an easy button risk scaling costly mistakes faster than they can catch them.
